# Experiment Design — Triggered Pirate Invasions and Survival of Hierarchical vs Non-Hierarchical Agents

**Status:** Design only. Nothing executed. No facts about empirical outcomes are asserted.
**Question:** *Does the triggering of built-in game mechanics, such as pirate invasions when a score threshold is reached, affect the survival durations of hierarchical versus non-hierarchical agents?*
**Deliverable contract:** A self-contained experiment design — rationale, controls, analysis plan, feasibility — that can be bound to any concrete engine whose mechanics match the Specimen contract defined below.

---

## 0. Document Map

1. Notation & Definitions Appendix (§1)
2. Specimen Sandbox — mechanic contract (§2)
3. Trigger Regimes (§3)
4. Agent Architectures with capacity-matching control (§4)
5. A priori causal rationale per regime (§5)
6. Experimental Design — mixed factorial, paired seeds, chequerboard (§6)
7. Outcome Metric — survival duration and censoring (§7)
8. Pre-registered analysis decision tree (§8)
9. Robustness & sensitivity (§9)
10. Sample-size justification (§10)
11. Feasibility — compute, storage, wall-clock, binding to a real engine (§11)
12. Threats-to-Validity table (§12)
13. Open issues / out-of-scope (§13)

---

## 1. Notation & Definitions Appendix

| Symbol | Definition | Default |
|---|---|---|
| $t$ | Discrete environment step index | $t \in \{0,1,\dots,H\}$ |
| $H$ | Episode horizon (steps); right-censor beyond | $H = 5000$ |
| $S_t$ | Score at step $t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ | — |
| $T$ | Trigger threshold | $T_{\text{mid}}$ (mid); sweep over $\{T_{\text{lo}}, T_{\text{mid}}, T_{\text{hi}}\}$ |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}$ | Regime: no trigger ever fires | — |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}$ | Regime: one raid wave at first crossing | — |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}$ | Regime: while $S_t \ge T$, raid every $K$ steps | $K = 200$ |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$ | Regime: one wave at first crossing, wave size $\propto \lfloor \alpha (S_t - T) \rfloor$ | $\alpha = 0.1$ |
| $K$ | Cadence for periodic regime | $200$ steps |
| $\alpha$ | Intensity slope for scaled regime | $0.1$ pirates / score-point overshoot |
| $\mathcal{A}_{\text{hier}}$ | Hierarchical (two-level subgoal) architecture cell | — |
| $\mathcal{A}_{\text{flat}}$ | Flat end-to-end policy architecture cell | — |
| $\mathcal{G}$ | Discrete subgoal set for hierarchical high-level policy | $\{\text{gather},\text{fortify},\text{evade},\text{counterattack}\}$ |
| $k_{\text{hl}}$ | High-level decision interval (steps) | $50$ |
| $n_s$ | Independent seeds per architecture × regime cell (primary) | $64$ |
| $m$ | Map layout (drawn from $\mathcal{M}$) | $\lvert\mathcal{M}\rvert = 8$ layouts |
| $\xi$ | RNG seed string (controls world init, event timing, all draws) | — |
| $\tau$ | Survival duration random variable | $\tau \in [0, H]$ |
| $\delta$ | Terminal failure indicator | $\delta = 1$ if failure, $0$ if censored at $H$ |
| $\text{RAID}_t$ | Boolean raid-active flag at step $t$ | — |
| $\Theta$ | Specimen parameter tuple $(T, K, \alpha, \text{raid\_size}, \text{raid\_dps}, \text{raid\_dur})$ | parameterizable |

**Naming convention.** *Architecture cell* = (architecture, regime). *Cell* = (architecture). The primary design has $2 \times 4 = 8$ architecture cells per threshold.

**Pin on "hierarchical."** A controller with a discrete high-level option submodule that emits a subgoal $g \in \mathcal{G}$ once every $k_{\text{hl}}$ steps, and a low-level submodule that emits a primitive action every step from $(o_t, g)$. **Pin on "non-hierarchical."** A single-module controller mapping $(o_t)\mapsto a_t$ with identical observation, action, and per-step budget conditions. (See §4 for capacity matching.)

---

## 2. Specimen Sandbox — Mechanic Contract

The Specimen is a formal mechanical specification, not a runnable artifact. The design can be bound to any real game iff that game's mechanics satisfy this contract.

### 2.1 World

- Discrete 2D toroidal grid, $32\times 32$, eight pre-defined layouts in $\mathcal{M}$ (one resource-clusters-near-base, one resource-clusters-distant, etc.).
- Agents: one player unit; base with HP/HP_base; up to $N_{\max}=24$ raider units.
- Resource nodes: harvested for score increments and HP restoration.

### 2.2 State & dynamics

- State $s_t = (\text{world}_t,\text{player}_t,\text{base}_t,\text{raiders}_t, S_t)$.
- Update rule is deterministic given $(\text{state}, \text{action}, \text{RNG draw})$.
- Per-step cost invariant across architectures (verified by side-channel timestamp on a held-out calibration harness).

### 2.3 Actions & observations

- Primitive action set $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim} = \{\text{move-N,E,S,W},\text{harvest},\text{fortify},\text{attack},\text{idle}\}$ (8 actions).
- Observation vector: spatial window around player, base HP, $S_t$, raider counts by distance bin, time-since-last-event.
- Identical for both architectures.

### 2.4 Score $S_t$

```
S_t = S_{t-1}
    + c_h * (resources_harvested_at_t)
    + c_m * (monument_value_if_completed)
    + c_s * (1 if alive and base intact, else 0)
```

Constants $(c_h, c_m, c_s)$ pinned; reported in the Specimen contract register.

### 2.5 Pirate-invasion mechanic

- Default state: $\text{RAID}_t = \text{false}$.
- Regime-specific dispatch rules (§3) determine when $\text{RAID}_t := \text{true}$.
- While $\text{RAID}_t = \text{true}$: spawn waves of size $W$ at distance band $d$, each raider dealing DPS $dpa$ for duration $D$ waves. $W, d, dpa, D$ pinned in regime definitions.
- Raiders expire after $D$ waves or after inflicting cumulative damage cap.

### 2.6 Terminal failure

- $\tau = t$ if at step $t$: player HP $\le 0$ **or** base HP $\le 0$.
- Else $\tau = H$, $\delta = 0$ (right-censored).

### 2.7 Initial-condition pins

- $S_0$ pinned below $T_{\text{lo}}$, identical across all cells.
- Identical initial resources, identical initial base HP, identical player HP.
- Identical map layouts drawn once from $\mathcal{M}$, then held fixed across architectures.

---

## 3. Trigger Regimes

| Regime | Dispatch rule | Cadence | Intensity |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}$ | $\text{RAID}_t \equiv \text{false}$ for all $t$ | none | none |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}$ | If $\neg\text{RAID}_{t-1}$ and $S_t \ge T$, set $\text{RAID}_t = \text{true}$ for one wave of size $W_0$ | one-shot | constant $W_0$ |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}$ | If $S_t \ge T$ and $(t - t_{\text{first\_cross}}) \mod K = 0$, spawn one wave | periodic, period $K$ | constant $W_0$ per wave |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$ | On first crossing spawn wave of size $W_0$; if wave resolved and $S_t \ge T$ still, re-arm to $\lceil \alpha (S_t - T) \rceil$ if larger | one-shot + escalator | $W \propto \lceil \alpha (S_t - T)\rceil$ |

**Defaults (pre-registered):** $K = 200$, $\alpha = 0.1$, $W_0 = 6$, raid DPS-profile and distance pin in contract register. **Robustness:** $K \in \{100, 200, 400\}$ and $\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$ reported as secondary sweeps in §9.

---

## 4. Agent Architectures & Capacity Matching (Hard Control)

### 4.1 Hierarchical architecture $\mathcal{A}_{\text{hier}}$

- **High-level policy** $\pi_{\text{high}}(g \mid o_{t:k_{\text{hl}}})$, discrete-softmax over $\mathcal{G}$.
- **Low-level policy** $\pi_{\text{low}}(a_t \mid o_t, g)$, with primitive action space $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim}$.
- High-level emits $g$ at steps $t \in \{0, k_{\text{hl}}, 2k_{\text{hl}}, \dots\}$; low-level emits one $a_t$ every step, including between high-level decisions (the previously committed $g$ persists).
- A separate value head $V_{\text{combined}}$ is used for training only and does not change the action distribution shape.

### 4.2 Non-hierarchical (flat) architecture $\mathcal{A}_{\text{flat}}$

- **Single policy** $\pi_{\text{flat}}(a_t \mid o_t)$ over $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim}$.
- A value head is included to mirror training conditions.

### 4.3 Capacity-matching control (hard)

To avoid confounding architecture with capacity, the following are **mandatory and pre-registered**:

| Axis | Constraint |
|---|---|
| Total trainable parameters $P$ | $\lvert P_{\text{hier}} - P_{\text{flat}}\rvert / P_{\text{flat}} \le 5\%$ |
| Optimizer family | identical (Adam) |
| Optimizer hyperparameters | identical $(\eta, \beta_1, \beta_2, \epsilon)$ |
| Update count (env steps per gradient step, total gradient steps) | identical |
| Replay memory | shared buffer length, identical sampling distribution |
| Exploration schedule | identical $(\epsilon_{\text{start}}, \epsilon_{\text{end}}, \text{decay})$ |
| Batch size | identical |
| Discount $\gamma$, TD$(\lambda)$ | identical |
| Random seed for init | shared seed and deterministic init order |

**Tolerance justification ($\pm 5\%$).** Implementations of "matched capacity" must contend with discretization of layer widths, embedding tables for $\mathcal{G}$, and head/tail asymmetries. A $\pm 5\%$ window on $P$ is tight enough to prevent gross capacity confounds (literature precedent in paired-network ablation design typically uses 5–10%) while permitting the natural parameter-count deltas introduced by embedding $\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert = 4$ discrete subgoals into the hierarchical encoder. As a robustness check, §9 reports results within a $\pm 2\%$ tight tolerance on a held-out subset; deviations in primary outcome between the $5\%$ and $2\%$ tolerances would be flagged and reported narratively.

### 4.4 Action-budget and timing-parity control

- Both architectures emit exactly one primitive action per environment step.
- Hierarchical emits $g$ at the pre-pinned $k_{\text{hl}}$ cadence; no additional actions, no skipping, no extra reads.
- Decision latency is irrelevant because both act synchronously with the environment step.

---

## 5. A priori Causal Rationale per Regime

For each regime, the design names the expected direction of the architecture effect, the mechanism, and the substantive alternative (the design must be able to detect either).

### 5.1 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}$ — no trigger

- **Expected direction (this design's prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} \approx \tau_{\text{flat}}$; either small flat underperformance from subgoal-switching overhead, or small hierarchical overperformance if subgoaling decomposes healthy-behaviour subproblems.
- **Mechanism:** no external stress tests the architecture's ability to schedule. Both controllers should maintain a baseline "gather without dying" loop.
- **Substantive alternative:** Hierarchical suffers from macro-level commitment to a subgoal across $k_{\text{hl}}$ steps when the optimal action is to immediately replan, so $\tau_{\text{hier}} < \tau_{\text{flat}}$.
- **Purpose in design:** arm acts as a control on capacity-only effects absent triggers; any Architecture main effect that survives only in regimes with triggers is interpretable as a triggered-mechanic interaction.

### 5.2 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}$ — one wave at threshold

- **Expected direction (prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} > \tau_{\text{flat}}$ by a moderate margin.
- **Mechanism:** the high-level controller can pre-commit to `fortify` (or stay in `fortify`) just before the crossed-threshold event if it has been collecting resources toward $T$; the flat policy must learn this anticipation purely from feature engineering over $(o_t, S_t)$.
- **Substantive alternative:** flat policy learns a sharp, low-latency mapping from $(S_{t-T}, \text{trajectory})$ to fortify action, and the hierarchical controller's fixed $k_{\text{hl}}$ cadence prevents it from anticipating the final pre-trigger decision in time.

### 5.3 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}$ — repeated raids

- **Expected direction (prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} > \tau_{\text{flat}}$ by a wider margin than $\mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}$; staggered adaptation benefits subgoal cycling.
- **Mechanism:** multi-step planning horizon at the macro level lets the controller weave `fortify` and `gather` in alternation across periods, exploiting high-level cadence; flat controller may thrash between conflicting primitive reflexes.
- **Substantive alternative:** commitment cost dominates — $\pi_{\text{high}}$ cannot reverse a stale subgoal within the $k_{\text{hl}}$ window, so the agent under-responds during the next wave's early phase; flat wins.

### 5.4 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$ — escalating intensity

- **Expected direction (prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} > \tau_{\text{flat}}$.
- **Mechanism:** hierarchical policy's subgoal space includes `evade` and `counterattack` as well as `gather` and `fortify`, so intensifying pressure maps cleanly onto a high-level switch; flat policy must learn a *continuous* scalar mapping from stress features to action probabilities, which is a harder credit-assignment problem.
- **Substantive alternative:** both architectures fail comparably under sustained DPS ramps; once any raid wave penetrates, the marginal value of architecture is small.

### 5.5 Causal graph

```
Architecture (HIER/FLAT)  ─┐
                            ├─► Behaviour pattern ─► Triggered event interaction ─► Survival τ
Triggering regime (4 arms) ─┘
      ↑
Deterministic schedule from paired seed ξ  (controls world init, event timing, all draws)
```

The Architecture × Regime interaction is the primary contrast of interest; the schedule contamination is closed by paired-seed replay (see §6).

---

## 6. Experimental Design

### 6.1 Factorial structure

- **Between-subjects factor:** Architecture ($\mathcal{A}_{\text{hier}}$ vs $\mathcal{A}_{\text{flat}}$).
- **Within-subjects factor:** Regime ($\mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$).
- **Threshold factor (robustness):** $T \in \{T_{\text{lo}}, T_{\text{mid}}, T_{\text{hi}}\}$, with $T_{\text{mid}}$ used for the *primary* analysis. The other two thresholds are reported as a robustness sweep.
- Cells per threshold: $2 \times 4 = 8$. Total architecture cells: $2 \times 4 \times 3 = 24$, but the primary analysis pool is $8$ cells × $T_{\text{mid}}$ alone.

### 6.2 Seed pairing

- Each seed index $i \in \{1, \dots, n_s\}$ defines one seed string $\xi_i$.
- For both architectures, the same $\xi_i$ determines: (i) world init, (ii) resource distribution, (iii) initial player & base state, (iv) any stochastic event timing that is *not* regime-defined (so the only regime-varying RNG draws come from the regime itself).
- Within $\xi_i$, the four regimes are presented in a **chequerboard (counterbalanced) order** across seeds, so any residual order effects are decorrelated from architecture.

### 6.3 Pre-registered defaults (from researcher authorization)

| Parameter | Default | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| $n_s$ (seeds per architecture cell) | $64$ | Achieves $\ge 30$ uncensored deaths in the smallest cell at $T_{\text{mid}}$ under realistic survival curves; power computed in §10. |
| $H$ (horizon) | $5000$ steps | Long enough that $\mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$ realize multi-event trajectories in most cells; short enough that compute remains tractable. |
| $T_{\text{mid}}, T_{\text{lo}}, T_{\text{hi}}$ | e.g. $\{0.45 S_{\max}, 0.30 S_{\max}, 0.60 S_{\max}\}$ calibrated so that half of seeds cross at $T_{\text{mid}}$ by step $H$ under $\mathcal{A}_{\text{flat}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}$. |
| Map pool $\mathcal{M}$ | $8$ fixed layouts, drawn once before the run | Avoids map-induced confound of architecture-with-layout. |

### 6.4 What is controlled across all cells

- Identical $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim}$; identical observation space; identical per-step budget; identical Specimen parameter pins.
- Identical optimizer, exploration, batch size, replay memory, training updates.
- Identical $S_0$, identical map layouts.
- Identical RNG seed string assigned to architecture & regime at the trial level via the seed protocol.

### 6.5 What *varies*

- Across rows of the $2 \times 4$ factorial, only (architecture, regime) vary.
- Across threshold-sweep cells, only $T$ varies; everything else held.

### 6.6 What *cannot* be controlled (and is acknowledged)

- Library-level RNG draws from non-rule-driven system paths (network is disabled; this is moot here). Documented in §12.

---

## 7. Outcome Metric — Survival Duration

**Primary outcome variable:** $\tau \in [0, H]$, the step at which terminal failure first occurs.

**Definition in the Specimen:**

$$\tau = \begin{cases} \min\{t : \text{playerHP}_t \le 0 \;\lor\; \text{baseHP}_t \le 0\}, & \text{otherwise} \\ H, & \text{if no failure by step } H \end{cases}$$

**Censoring indicator:** $\delta = \mathbb{1}[\tau < H]$.

**Right-censoring rule:** when $\tau = H$, the censored observation contributes under standard survival-analysis weighting; KM and Cox estimators handle this natively.

**Censoring at horizon cap.** A right-censoring fraction under $25\%$ is targeted per cell to avoid informative-censoring bias; if a cell exceeds $30\%$ censoring, KM tail extrapolation (exponential tail fit on the last decile) is reported as a robustness view in §9. The horizon bound $H = 5000$ is set with this target in mind.

**Auxiliary outcomes (secondary, pre-registered):**

- $\tau_{\text{to-event}}$: steps from episode start to first event (single, periodic wave 1, scaled wave 1). Diagnostic only — not a Primary.
- $n_{\text{waves-survived}}$: count of waves survived before terminal failure.
- $\text{score-ceiling}_\tau = S_\tau$: terminal score.

These are reported to characterize mechanism, not to adjudicate the primary question.

---

## 8. Pre-registered Analysis Decision Tree

```
PRIMARY OUTCOME
  └─ τ (survival duration in [0, H]), right-censored at H

PRIMARY CONTRAST
  └─ Architecture × Regime interaction (does τ_hier − τ_flat depend on regime?)

PRIMARY TEST
  └─ Mixed-effects Cox proportional-hazards model:
       h(t | X, ξ_i) = h_0(t) · exp(β_arch · arch + β_regime · regime
                                    + β_int · (arch × regime) + u_ξ_i)
     random intercept u_ξ_i ~ N(0, σ²_ξ) on seed ξ_i
     Reports: HR_arch, HR_regime, HR_int each with 95% CI; p_int pre-registered
  └─ If Schoenfeld residuals reject proportional-hazards assumption:
     → Stratified Cox by regime (collapse interaction test).
     Pre-registered fallback.
  └─ Non-parametric check: stratified log-rank test across regimes, by architecture.

SECONDARY CONTRASTS (pre-registered list, Holm-Bonferroni adjusted)
  1. Architecture main effect (collapsed across regime)
  2. Regime main effect (collapsed across architecture)
  3. Within-architecture pairwise regime contrasts (3 per architecture, 6 total)
  4. Subgroup HR at each regime level

EXPLORATORY CONTRASTS (not pre-registered, marked exploratory in any write-up)
  - Threshold-level subgroup analyses
  - Seed-cluster analyses (leave-one-seed-out)
  - Wave-count covariate models

MISSING DATA HANDLING
  └─ Design is seed-complete: missingness equals zero by construction.
  └─ In the event of run-level failures (e.g. Specimen contract violation
     detected post-hoc), the affected seed is excluded and a sensitivity
     re-run is reported with results from a deviance threshold in §9.

CENSORING TREATMENT
  └─ Right-censoring at H handled by Cox and KM estimators natively.
  └─ Censoring-fraction diagnostic per cell; >30% triggers exponential-tail
     robustness view (KM tail extrapolation).

MULTIPLICITY RULE
  └─ Holm-Bonferroni step-down over the 4 secondary contrast families.
  └─ Primary interaction tested at α = 0.05 and reported regardless of
     multiplicity adjustment.

EFFECT-SIZE REPORTING
  └─ Hazard ratio with 95% CI is the primary effect size for τ.
  └─ Cohen's d on log(τ + 1) reported as a familiar secondary effect size.
  └─ Median survival and 25th/75th percentiles reported per cell.

ROBUSTNESS PRIORITIZATION
  └─ Pre-registered order: (a) threshold sweep, (b) capacity-tolerance tightening,
     (c) censoring-fraction sensitivity, (d) leave-one-seed-out, (e) bootstrap CI
     over seeds.
```

**Decision rule for adjudicating the primary question.** The question is about whether the *triggering of mechanics* affects the survival of hierarchical vs non-hierarchical agents. We adjudicate as follows:

- If the Architecture × Regime interaction in the Cox model reaches $\alpha = 0.05$ with $|HR_{\text{int}}| \not\approx 1$, the answer is **yes** (the survival difference between architectures depends on regime).
- If the interaction fails but Architecture main effect survives Holm-corrected secondary tests *and* all four regimes show monotone direction-consistent HIER-vs-FLAT HRs, report **provisionally yes** with the architecture main effect conditional on regime.
- If neither interaction nor main effect reaches significance, report **insufficient evidence** and explicitly identify power under $n_s = 64$ (computed in §10).

---

## 9. Robustness & Sensitivity

| Check | What it varies | Decision criteria |
|---|---|---|
| Threshold sweep | $T \in \{T_{\text{lo}}, T_{\text{mid}}, T_{\text{hi}}\}$ | Primary direction of $HR_{\text{int}}$ is consistent across at least 2 of 3 thresholds |
| Capacity-tolerance tightening | $\pm 5\% \to \pm 2\%$ on parameter count | Direction preserved; magnitude variation reported as confidence band |
| Subgoal cadence sweep | $k_{\text{hl}} \in \{25, 50, 100\}$ (hierarchical only) | Direction preserved; magnitude reported as robustness band |
| Cadence $K$ sweep | $K \in \{100, 200, 400\}$ (periodic regime) | Direction preserved |
| Intensity $\alpha$ sweep | $\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$ (scaled regime) | Direction preserved |
| Censoring sensitivity | KM tail extrapolation if censoring $> 30\%$ | Disagreement triggers caveat narrative |
| Leave-one-seed-out | Repeat with one seed removed | No single seed drives the effect |
| Bootstrap CIs | Resample seeds 10,000 times | 95% CI on HR; reported with point estimate |
| Map robustness | Repeat with maps sampled from a held-out pool of 4 | Direction preserved across maps |

Specific defaults: $H=5000$, $n_s=64$ — these are sensitivity-tunable. §10 considers $n_s \in \{32, 64, 96\}$ and $H \in \{3000, 5000, 8000\}$.

---

## 10. Sample-Size Justification

### 10.1 Pre-registered prospective rule

Each architecture cell must reach **at least 30 uncensored deaths (i.e., $\delta = 1$)** *or* the Kaplan–Meier standard error on the median survival must fall below a pre-specified precision target under realistic survival curves.

### 10.2 Worked power estimate (analytical, not empirical)

Assume an exponential baseline survival with median $\tau_0 = 1500$ steps, $H = 5000$, so expected uncensoring fraction $\approx 1 - \exp(-H/\tau_0) \approx 1 - \exp(-3.33) \approx 0.964$. With $n_s = 64$ per cell, expected deaths $\approx 62$, well above the 30 threshold. If the relevant survival is shorter (e.g., $\tau_0 = 700$, which models the worst regime), uncensoring $\approx 1 - \exp(-5000/700) \approx 0.999$, so $n_s = 64$ again exceeds the 30-death threshold.

For Cox detection of an interaction effect size of $HR_{\text{int}} = 1.5$ with two-sided $\alpha = 0.05$, power $\approx 0.85$ at $n_s = 64$ per architecture cell under the rule-of-thumb that $10$ events-per-coefficient are needed (Hsieh–Lavori-style). Realized event counts substantially exceed that under any of the survival curves above. Smaller interactions ($HR_{\text{int}} = 1.25$) would require $n_s \approx 96$ to retain $0.80$ power.

### 10.3 Sensitivity to defaults

| $(n_s, H)$ combination | Satisfies ≥30 deaths / cell? | Power vs $HR_{\text{int}}=1.5$ | Power vs $HR_{\text{int}}=1.25$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(32, 3000)$ | Boundary; report flag | $\approx 0.60$ | $\approx 0.25$ |
| **(64, 5000)** (default) | Yes | $\approx 0.85$ | $\approx 0.45$ |
| $(96, 5000)$ | Yes | $\approx 0.95$ | $\approx 0.65$ |
| $(64, 8000)$ | Yes | $\approx 0.88$ | $\approx 0.50$ |

The pre-registered default $(64, 5000)$ is selected as the design's primary anchor; §9 reports sensitivity to both $n_s$ and $H$.

---

## 11. Feasibility

This section reports numerical *targets*, not execution claims. All values are design-stage estimates derived from the Specimen contract; binding to a real engine changes them.

### 11.1 Compute-hours target

- **Per-trial simulation time** (Specimen reference speed, Java/Python reference profile):
  - $H = 5000$ steps × $\approx 50\,\mu$s/step (StepsC++ reference) $\Rightarrow$ $\approx 0.25$ s/trial.
- **Per architecture cell:** $n_s \cdot 4 \text{ regimes} \cdot 0.25 \text{ s} = 64 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.25 = 64$ s.
- **All primary cells:** $2$ arch × $4$ reg × $64$ s = $512$ s ≈ $0.14$ hours of pure simulation.
- **All cells including threshold sweep:** $0.14 \times 3 = 0.43$ hours.
- **Policy training (offline, not part of per-trial compute):**
  - Estimate: $4$ hours per trained policy on 24-thread CPU (no GPU required).
  - Policies required: $2$ architectures × $1$ training corpus = $2$ policies.
  - Total training: $\approx 8$ hours.
  - Note: if the Specimen is bound to a learned-agent framework that requires retraining per regime, multiply accordingly; in the default Specimen, regime is an environment configuration toggle, not an agent retraining condition.
- **Total runtime target:** $\approx 8$–$10$ hours wall-clock to produce primary analysis on a 24-core CPU.

### 11.2 Wall-clock rationale

- 24-core CPU affinity is sufficient because: (i) trials are independent across seeds and can be parallelized one trial per core; (ii) per-trial memory is small (§11.3).
- Wall-clock target is dominated by training (8h) over per-trial simulation (~0.5h). Training is sequential within a policy but parallelizable across the two architectures.

### 11.3 Storage footprint target

- Per-trial log: $\approx 32$ bytes/step × $H$ steps = $160$ KB.
- Per architecture cell: $64$ s × $4$ regimes × $160$ KB ≈ $40$ MB.
- All architecture cells primary: $2 \times 4 \times 40 = 320$ MB.
- All architecture cells including sweep: $\approx 1$ GB.
- Including model checkpoints ($\approx 50$ MB per trained policy × $\approx 8$ policies) and analysis tables: **total target storage bear ≤ 5 GB.**

### 11.4 Bind to real engine

To execute the design against a real (closed or open) game:

1. Verify the game's mechanics match the Specimen contract (§2).
2. Where the game exposes official hooks (e.g., event triggers, damage tables), map them to Specimen pins.
3. Implement an adapter that exposes: $\text{score}_t$, $\text{failure}_t$, $\text{raid}_t$, $\text{terminate}$ as observations/actions.
4. Replay the seed protocol; ensure all RNG draws route through the central $\xi_i$ so seed parity holds.
5. Re-run the budget with the *real* per-step timing.

If the engine does not expose the exact mechanic contract (e.g., trigger is probability-scaled rather than threshold-deterministic, or raids are deterministic not stochastic), the Specimen must be re-parameterized or the design relaxed — and this is recorded as a construct-validity threat in §12.

### 11.5 Out of scope (not budget)

- GPU-based environments.
- Networked multi-agent settings.
- Human-in-the-loop evaluations.
- Adversarial agents (raider behavior is environment-controlled).

---

## 12. Threats-to-Validity Table

| # | Type | Threat | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Internal | Threshold pre-period scoring differs across cells | Identical $S_0$, identical map layouts, identical exploration; pre-trigger $\tau_{\text{to-event}}$ reported as a diagnostic; if imbalance exceeds $1\sigma$, covariate-adjusted Cox reported in §9 |
| T2 | Internal | RNG contamination from non-rule-driven draws | Single RNG source routed through $\xi_i$; deterministic replay; checksum on world init; verification log |
| T3 | Internal | Capacity mismatch between architectures | $\pm 5\%$ parameter tolerance with $\pm 2\%$ sensitivity; matched optimizer, exploration, batch size, replay |

## 2. Specimen Sandbox — Mechanic Contract

The Specimen is a formal mechanical specification, not a runnable artifact. The design can be bound to any real game iff that game's mechanics satisfy this contract.

### 2.1 World

- Discrete 2D toroidal grid, $32\times 32$, eight pre-defined layouts in $\mathcal{M}$ (one resource-clusters-near-base, one resource-clusters-distant, etc.).
- Agents: one player unit; base with HP/HP_base; up to $N_{\max}=24$ raider units.
- Resource nodes: harvested for score increments and HP restoration.

### 2.2 State & dynamics

- State $s_t = (\text{world}_t,\text{player}_t,\text{base}_t,\text{raiders}_t, S_t)$.
- Update rule is deterministic given $(\text{state}, \text{action}, \text{RNG draw})$.
- Per-step cost invariant across architectures (verified by side-channel timestamp on a held-out calibration harness).

### 2.3 Actions & observations

- Primitive action set $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim} = \{\text{move-N,E,S,W},\text{harvest},\text{fortify},\text{attack},\text{idle}\}$ (8 actions).
- Observation vector: spatial window around player, base HP, $S_t$, raider counts by distance bin, time-since-last-event.
- Identical for both architectures.

### 2.4 Score $S_t$

```
S_t = S_{t-1}
    + c_h * (resources_harvested_at_t)
    + c_m * (monument_value_if_completed)
    + c_s * (1 if alive and base intact, else 0)
```

Constants $(c_h, c_m, c_s)$ pinned; reported in the Specimen contract register.

### 2.5 Pirate-invasion mechanic

- Default state: $\text{RAID}_t = \text{false}$.
- Regime-specific dispatch rules (§3) determine when $\text{RAID}_t := \text{true}$.
- While $\text{RAID}_t = \text{true}$: spawn waves of size $W$ at distance band $d$, each raider dealing DPS $dpa$ for duration $D$ waves. $W, d, dpa, D$ pinned in regime definitions.
- Raiders expire after $D$ waves or after inflicting cumulative damage cap.

### 2.6 Terminal failure

- $\tau = t$ if at step $t$: player HP $\le 0$ **or** base HP $\le 0$.
- Else $\tau = H$, $\delta = 0$ (right-censored).

### 2.7 Initial-condition pins

- $S_0$ pinned below $T_{\text{lo}}$, identical across all cells.
- Identical initial resources, identical initial base HP, identical player HP.
- Identical map layouts drawn once from $\mathcal{M}$, then held fixed across architectures.

## 3. Trigger Regimes

| Regime | Dispatch rule | Cadence | Intensity |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}$ | $\text{RAID}_t \equiv \text{false}$ for all $t$ | none | none |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}$ | If $\neg\text{RAID}_{t-1}$ and $S_t \ge T$, set $\text{RAID}_t = \text{true}$ for one wave of size $W_0$ | one-shot | constant $W_0$ |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}$ | If $S_t \ge T$ and $(t - t_{\text{first\_cross}}) \mod K = 0$, spawn one wave | periodic, period $K$ | constant $W_0$ per wave |
| $\mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$ | On first crossing spawn wave of size $W_0$; if wave resolved and $S_t \ge T$ still, re-arm to $\lceil \alpha (S_t - T) \rceil$ if larger | one-shot + escalator | $W \propto \lceil \alpha (S_t - T)\rceil$ |

**Defaults (pre-registered):** $K = 200$, $\alpha = 0.1$, $W_0 = 6$, raid DPS-profile and distance pin in contract register. **Robustness:** $K \in \{100, 200, 400\}$ and $\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$ reported as secondary sweeps in §9.

## 4. Agent Architectures & Capacity Matching (Hard Control)

### 4.1 Hierarchical architecture $\mathcal{A}_{\text{hier}}$

- **High-level policy** $\pi_{\text{high}}(g \mid o_{t:k_{\text{hl}}})$, discrete-softmax over $\mathcal{G}$.
- **Low-level policy** $\pi_{\text{low}}(a_t \mid o_t, g)$, with primitive action space $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim}$.
- High-level emits $g$ at steps $t \in \{0, k_{\text{hl}}, 2k_{\text{hl}}, \dots\}$; low-level emits one $a_t$ every step, including between high-level decisions (the previously committed $g$ persists).
- A separate value head $V_{\text{combined}}$ is used for training only and does not change the action distribution shape.

### 4.2 Non-hierarchical (flat) architecture $\mathcal{A}_{\text{flat}}$

- **Single policy** $\pi_{\text{flat}}(a_t \mid o_t)$ over $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim}$.
- A value head is included to mirror training conditions.

### 4.3 Capacity-matching control (hard)

To avoid confounding architecture with capacity, the following are **mandatory and pre-registered**:

| Axis | Constraint |
|---|---|
| Total trainable parameters $P$ | $\lvert P_{\text{hier}} - P_{\text{flat}}\rvert / P_{\text{flat}} \le 5\%$ |
| Optimizer family | identical (Adam) |
| Optimizer hyperparameters | identical $(\eta, \beta_1, \beta_2, \epsilon)$ |
| Update count (env steps per gradient step, total gradient steps) | identical |
| Replay memory | shared buffer length, identical sampling distribution |
| Exploration schedule | identical $(\epsilon_{\text{start}}, \epsilon_{\text{end}}, \text{decay})$ |
| Batch size | identical |
| Discount $\gamma$, TD$(\lambda)$ | identical |
| Random seed for init | shared seed and deterministic init order |

**Tolerance justification ($\pm 5\%$).** Implementations of "matched capacity" must contend with discretization of layer widths, embedding tables for $\mathcal{G}$, and head/tail asymmetries. A $\pm 5\%$ window on $P$ is tight enough to prevent gross capacity confounds (literature precedent in paired-network ablation design typically uses 5–10%) while permitting the natural parameter-count deltas introduced by embedding $\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert = 4$ discrete subgoals into the hierarchical encoder. As a robustness check, §9 reports results within a $\pm 2\%$ tight tolerance on a held-out subset; deviations in primary outcome between the $5\%$ and $2\%$ tolerances would be flagged and reported narratively.

### 4.4 Action-budget and timing-parity control

- Both architectures emit exactly one primitive action per environment step.
- Hierarchical emits $g$ at the pre-pinned $k_{\text{hl}}$ cadence; no additional actions, no skipping, no extra reads.
- Decision latency is irrelevant because both act synchronously with the environment step.

## 5. A priori Causal Rationale per Regime

For each regime, the design names the expected direction of the architecture effect, the mechanism, and the substantive alternative (the design must be able to detect either).

### 5.1 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}$ — no trigger

- **Expected direction (this design's prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} \approx \tau_{\text{flat}}$; either small flat underperformance from subgoal-switching overhead, or small hierarchical overperformance if subgoaling decomposes healthy-behaviour subproblems.
- **Mechanism:** no external stress tests the architecture's ability to schedule. Both controllers should maintain a baseline "gather without dying" loop.
- **Substantive alternative:** Hierarchical suffers from macro-level commitment to a subgoal across $k_{\text{hl}}$ steps when the optimal action is to immediately replan, so $\tau_{\text{hier}} < \tau_{\text{flat}}$.
- **Purpose in design:** arm acts as a control on capacity-only effects absent triggers; any Architecture main effect that survives only in regimes with triggers is interpretable as a triggered-mechanic interaction.

### 5.2 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}$ — one wave at threshold

- **Expected direction (prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} > \tau_{\text{flat}}$ by a moderate margin.
- **Mechanism:** the high-level controller can pre-commit to `fortify` (or stay in `fortify`) just before the crossed-threshold event if it has been collecting resources toward $T$; the flat policy must learn this anticipation purely from feature engineering over $(o_t, S_t)$.
- **Substantive alternative:** flat policy learns a sharp, low-latency mapping from $(S_{t-T}, \text{trajectory})$ to fortify action, and the hierarchical controller's fixed $k_{\text{hl}}$ cadence prevents it from anticipating the final pre-trigger decision in time.

### 5.3 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}$ — repeated raids

- **Expected direction (prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} > \tau_{\text{flat}}$ by a wider margin than $\mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}$; staggered adaptation benefits subgoal cycling.
- **Mechanism:** multi-step planning horizon at the macro level lets the controller weave `fortify` and `gather` in alternation across periods, exploiting high-level cadence; flat controller may thrash between conflicting primitive reflexes.
- **Substantive alternative:** commitment cost dominates — $\pi_{\text{high}}$ cannot reverse a stale subgoal within the $k_{\text{hl}}$ window, so the agent under-responds during the next wave's early phase; flat wins.

### 5.4 $\mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$ — escalating intensity

- **Expected direction (prior):** $\tau_{\text{hier}} > \tau_{\text{flat}}$.
- **Mechanism:** hierarchical policy's subgoal space includes `evade` and `counterattack` as well as `gather` and `fortify`, so intensifying pressure maps cleanly onto a high-level switch; flat policy must learn a *continuous* scalar mapping from stress features to action probabilities, which is a harder credit-assignment problem.
- **Substantive alternative:** both architectures fail comparably under sustained DPS ramps; once any raid wave penetrates, the marginal value of architecture is small.

### 5.5 Causal graph

```
Architecture (HIER/FLAT)  ─┐
                            ├─► Behaviour pattern ─► Triggered event interaction ─► Survival τ
Triggering regime (4 arms) ─┘
      ↑
Deterministic schedule from paired seed ξ  (controls world init, event timing, all draws)
```

The Architecture × Regime interaction is the primary contrast of interest; the schedule contamination is closed by paired-seed replay (see §6).

## 6. Experimental Design

### 6.1 Factorial structure

- **Between-subjects factor:** Architecture ($\mathcal{A}_{\text{hier}}$ vs $\mathcal{A}_{\text{flat}}$).
- **Within-subjects factor:** Regime ($\mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{single}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$).
- **Threshold factor (robustness):** $T \in \{T_{\text{lo}}, T_{\text{mid}}, T_{\text{hi}}\}$, with $T_{\text{mid}}$ used for the *primary* analysis. The other two thresholds are reported as a robustness sweep.
- Cells per threshold: $2 \times 4 = 8$. Total architecture cells: $2 \times 4 \times 3 = 24$, but the primary analysis pool is $8$ cells × $T_{\text{mid}}$ alone.

### 6.2 Seed pairing

- Each seed index $i \in \{1, \dots, n_s\}$ defines one seed string $\xi_i$.
- For both architectures, the same $\xi_i$ determines: (i) world init, (ii) resource distribution, (iii) initial player & base state, (iv) any stochastic event timing that is *not* regime-defined (so the only regime-varying RNG draws come from the regime itself).
- Within $\xi_i$, the four regimes are presented in a **chequerboard (counterbalanced) order** across seeds, so any residual order effects are decorrelated from architecture.

### 6.3 Pre-registered defaults (from researcher authorization)

| Parameter | Default | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| $n_s$ (seeds per architecture cell) | $64$ | Achieves $\ge 30$ uncensored deaths in the smallest cell at $T_{\text{mid}}$ under realistic survival curves; power computed in §10. |
| $H$ (horizon) | $5000$ steps | Long enough that $\mathcal{R}_{\text{period}}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{\text{scaled}}$ realize multi-event trajectories in most cells; short enough that compute remains tractable. |
| $T_{\text{mid}}, T_{\text{lo}}, T_{\text{hi}}$ | e.g. $\{0.45 S_{\max}, 0.30 S_{\max}, 0.60 S_{\max}\}$ calibrated so that half of seeds cross at $T_{\text{mid}}$ by step $H$ under $\mathcal{A}_{\text{flat}}, \mathcal{R}_{\text{off}}$. |
| Map pool $\mathcal{M}$ | $8$ fixed layouts, drawn once before the run | Avoids map-induced confound of architecture-with-layout. |

### 6.4 What is controlled across all cells

- Identical $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim}$; identical observation space; identical per-step budget; identical Specimen parameter pins.
- Identical optimizer, exploration, batch size, replay memory, training updates.
- Identical $S_0$, identical map layouts.
- Identical RNG seed string assigned to architecture & regime at the trial level via the seed protocol.

### 6.5 What *varies*

- Across rows of the $2 \times 4$ factorial, only (architecture, regime) vary.
- Across threshold-sweep cells, only $T$ varies; everything else held.

### 6.6 What *cannot* be controlled (and is acknowledged)

- Library-level RNG draws from non-rule-driven system paths (network is disabled; this is moot here). Documented in §12.

## 7. Outcome Metric — Survival Duration

**Primary outcome variable:** $\tau \in [0, H]$, the step at which terminal failure first occurs.

**Definition in the Specimen:**

$$\tau = \begin{cases} \min\{t : \text{playerHP}_t \le 0 \;\lor\; \text{baseHP}_t \le 0\}, & \text{otherwise} \\ H, & \text{if no failure by step } H \end{cases}$$

**Censoring indicator:** $\delta = \mathbb{1}[\tau < H]$.

**Right-censoring rule:** when $\tau = H$, the censored observation contributes under standard survival-analysis weighting; KM and Cox estimators handle this natively.

**Censoring at horizon cap.** A right-censoring fraction under $25\%$ is targeted per cell to avoid informative-censoring bias; if a cell exceeds $30\%$ censoring, KM tail extrapolation (exponential tail fit on the last decile) is reported as a robustness view in §9. The horizon bound $H = 5000$ is set with this target in mind.

**Auxiliary outcomes (secondary, pre-registered):**

- $\tau_{\text{to-event}}$: steps from episode start to first event (single, periodic wave 1, scaled wave 1). Diagnostic only — not a Primary.
- $n_{\text{waves-survived}}$: count of waves survived before terminal failure.
- $\text{score-ceiling}_\tau = S_\tau$: terminal score.

These are reported to characterize mechanism, not to adjudicate the primary question.

## 8. Pre-registered Analysis Decision Tree

```
PRIMARY OUTCOME
  └─ τ (survival duration in [0, H]), right-censored at H

PRIMARY CONTRAST
  └─ Architecture × Regime interaction (does τ_hier − τ_flat depend on regime?)

PRIMARY TEST
  └─ Mixed-effects Cox proportional-hazards model:
       h(t | X, ξ_i) = h_0(t) · exp(β_arch · arch + β_regime · regime
                                    + β_int · (arch × regime) + u_ξ_i)
     random intercept u_ξ_i ~ N(0, σ²_ξ) on seed ξ_i
     Reports: HR_arch, HR_regime, HR_int each with 95% CI; p_int pre-registered
  └─ If Schoenfeld residuals reject proportional-hazards assumption:
     → Stratified Cox by regime (collapse interaction test).
     Pre-registered fallback.
  └─ Non-parametric check: stratified log-rank test across regimes, by architecture.

SECONDARY CONTRASTS (pre-registered list, Holm-Bonferroni adjusted)
  1. Architecture main effect (collapsed across regime)
  2. Regime main effect (collapsed across architecture)
  3. Within-architecture pairwise regime contrasts (3 per architecture, 6 total)
  4. Subgroup HR at each regime level

EXPLORATORY CONTRASTS (not pre-registered, marked exploratory in any write-up)
  - Threshold-level subgroup analyses
  - Seed-cluster analyses (leave-one-seed-out)
  - Wave-count covariate models

MISSING DATA HANDLING
  └─ Design is seed-complete: missingness equals zero by construction.
  └─ In the event of run-level failures (e.g. Specimen contract violation
     detected post-hoc), the affected seed is excluded and a sensitivity
     re-run is reported with results from a deviance threshold in §9.

CENSORING TREATMENT
  └─ Right-censoring at H handled by Cox and KM estimators natively.
  └─ Censoring-fraction diagnostic per cell; >30% triggers exponential-tail
     robustness view (KM tail extrapolation).

MULTIPLICITY RULE
  └─ Holm-Bonferroni step-down over the 4 secondary contrast families.
  └─ Primary interaction tested at α = 0.05 and reported regardless of
     multiplicity adjustment.

EFFECT-SIZE REPORTING
  └─ Hazard ratio with 95% CI is the primary effect size for τ.
  └─ Cohen's d on log(τ + 1) reported as a familiar secondary effect size.
  └─ Median survival and 25th/75th percentiles reported per cell.

ROBUSTNESS PRIORITIZATION
  └─ Pre-registered order: (a) threshold sweep, (b) capacity-tolerance tightening,
     (c) censoring-fraction sensitivity, (d) leave-one-seed-out, (e) bootstrap CI
     over seeds.
```

**Decision rule for adjudicating the primary question.** The question is about whether the *triggering of mechanics* affects the survival of hierarchical vs non-hierarchical agents. We adjudicate as follows:

- If the Architecture × Regime interaction in the Cox model reaches $\alpha = 0.05$ with $|HR_{\text{int}}| \not\approx 1$, the answer is **yes** (the survival difference between architectures depends on regime).
- If the interaction fails but Architecture main effect survives Holm-corrected secondary tests *and* all four regimes show monotone direction-consistent HIER-vs-FLAT HRs, report **provisionally yes** with the architecture main effect conditional on regime.
- If neither interaction nor main effect reaches significance, report **insufficient evidence** and explicitly identify power under $n_s = 64$ (computed in §10).

## 9. Robustness & Sensitivity

| Check | What it varies | Decision criteria |
|---|---|---|
| Threshold sweep | $T \in \{T_{\text{lo}}, T_{\text{mid}}, T_{\text{hi}}\}$ | Primary direction of $HR_{\text{int}}$ is consistent across at least 2 of 3 thresholds |
| Capacity-tolerance tightening | $\pm 5\% \to \pm 2\%$ on parameter count | Direction preserved; magnitude variation reported as confidence band |
| Subgoal cadence sweep | $k_{\text{hl}} \in \{25, 50, 100\}$ (hierarchical only) | Direction preserved; magnitude reported as robustness band |
| Cadence $K$ sweep | $K \in \{100, 200, 400\}$ (periodic regime) | Direction preserved |
| Intensity $\alpha$ sweep | $\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$ (scaled regime) | Direction preserved |
| Censoring sensitivity | KM tail extrapolation if censoring $> 30\%$ | Disagreement triggers caveat narrative |
| Leave-one-seed-out | Repeat with one seed removed | No single seed drives the effect |
| Bootstrap CIs | Resample seeds 10,000 times | 95% CI on HR; reported with point estimate |
| Map robustness | Repeat with maps sampled from a held-out pool of 4 | Direction preserved across maps |

Specific defaults: $H=5000$, $n_s=64$ — these are sensitivity-tunable. §10 considers $n_s \in \{32, 64, 96\}$ and $H \in \{3000, 5000, 8000\}$.

## 10. Sample-Size Justification

### 10.1 Pre-registered prospective rule

Each architecture cell must reach **at least 30 uncensored deaths (i.e., $\delta = 1$)** *or* the Kaplan–Meier standard error on the median survival must fall below a pre-specified precision target under realistic survival curves.

### 10.2 Worked power estimate (analytical, not empirical)

Assume an exponential baseline survival with median $\tau_0 = 1500$ steps, $H = 5000$, so expected uncensoring fraction $\approx 1 - \exp(-H/\tau_0) \approx 1 - \exp(-3.33) \approx 0.964$. With $n_s = 64$ per cell, expected deaths $\approx 62$, well above the 30 threshold. If the relevant survival is shorter (e.g., $\tau_0 = 700$, which models the worst regime), uncensoring $\approx 1 - \exp(-5000/700) \approx 0.999$, so $n_s = 64$ again exceeds the 30-death threshold.

For Cox detection of an interaction effect size of $HR_{\text{int}} = 1.5$ with two-sided $\alpha = 0.05$, power $\approx 0.85$ at $n_s = 64$ per architecture cell under the rule-of-thumb that $10$ events-per-coefficient are needed (Hsieh–Lavori-style). Realized event counts substantially exceed that under any of the survival curves above. Smaller interactions ($HR_{\text{int}} = 1.25$) would require $n_s \approx 96$ to retain $0.80$ power.

### 10.3 Sensitivity to defaults

| $(n_s, H)$ combination | Satisfies ≥30 deaths / cell? | Power vs $HR_{\text{int}}=1.5$ | Power vs $HR_{\text{int}}=1.25$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(32, 3000)$ | Boundary; report flag | $\approx 0.60$ | $\approx 0.25$ |
| **(64, 5000)** (default) | Yes | $\approx 0.85$ | $\approx 0.45$ |
| $(96, 5000)$ | Yes | $\approx 0.95$ | $\approx 0.65$ |
| $(64, 8000)$ | Yes | $\approx 0.88$ | $\approx 0.50$ |

The pre-registered default $(64, 5000)$ is selected as the design's primary anchor; §9 reports sensitivity to both $n_s$ and $H$.

## 11. Feasibility

This section reports numerical *targets*, not execution claims. All values are design-stage estimates derived from the Specimen contract; binding to a real engine changes them.

### 11.1 Compute-hours target

- **Per-trial simulation time** (Specimen reference speed, Java/Python reference profile):
  - $H = 5000$ steps × $\approx 50\,\mu$s/step (StepsC++ reference) $\Rightarrow$ $\approx 0.25$ s/trial.
- **Per architecture cell:** $n_s \cdot 4 \text{ regimes} \cdot 0.25 \text{ s} = 64 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.25 = 64$ s.
- **All primary cells:** $2$ arch × $4$ reg × $64$ s = $512$ s ≈ $0.14$ hours of pure simulation.
- **All cells including threshold sweep:** $0.14 \times 3 = 0.43$ hours.
- **Policy training (offline, not part of per-trial compute):**
  - Estimate: $4$ hours per trained policy on 24-thread CPU (no GPU required).
  - Policies required: $2$ architectures × $1$ training corpus = $2$ policies.
  - Total training: $\approx 8$ hours.
  - Note: if the Specimen is bound to a learned-agent framework that requires retraining per regime, multiply accordingly; in the default Specimen, regime is an environment configuration toggle, not an agent retraining condition.
- **Total runtime target:** $\approx 8$–$10$ hours wall-clock to produce primary analysis on a 24-core CPU.

### 11.2 Wall-clock rationale

- 24-core CPU affinity is sufficient because: (i) trials are independent across seeds and can be parallelized one trial per core; (ii) per-trial memory is small (§11.3).
- Wall-clock target is dominated by training (8h) over per-trial simulation (~0.5h). Training is sequential within a policy but parallelizable across the two architectures.

### 11.3 Storage footprint target

- Per-trial log: $\approx 32$ bytes/step × $H$ steps = $160$ KB.
- Per architecture cell: $64$ s × $4$ regimes × $160$ KB ≈ $40$ MB.
- All architecture cells primary: $2 \times 4 \times 40 = 320$ MB.
- All architecture cells including sweep: $\approx 1$ GB.
- Including model checkpoints ($\approx 50$ MB per trained policy × $\approx 8$ policies) and analysis tables: **total target storage bear ≤ 5 GB.**

### 11.4 Bind to real engine

To execute the design against a real (closed or open) game:

1. Verify the game's mechanics match the Specimen contract (§2).
2. Where the game exposes official hooks (e.g., event triggers, damage tables), map them to Specimen pins.
3. Implement an adapter that exposes: $\text{score}_t$, $\text{failure}_t$, $\text{raid}_t$, $\text{terminate}$ as observations/actions.
4. Replay the seed protocol; ensure all RNG draws route through the central $\xi_i$ so seed parity holds.
5. Re-run the budget with the *real* per-step timing.

If the engine does not expose the exact mechanic contract (e.g., trigger is probability-scaled rather than threshold-deterministic, or raids are deterministic not stochastic), the Specimen must be re-parameterized or the design relaxed — and this is recorded as a construct-validity threat in §12.

### 11.5 Out of scope (not budget)

- GPU-based environments.
- Networked multi-agent settings.
- Human-in-the-loop evaluations.
- Adversarial agents (raider behavior is environment-controlled).

## 13. Open Issues / Out-of-Scope

- **Engine binding.** This design assumes Specimen contract holds; real-engine binding requires verification + adapter development.
- **Action-space generalizability.** If a real engine has a richer action space than $\mathcal{A}_\text{prim}$ (e.g., continuous actions, multi-unit commands), the hierarchical subgoal space $\mathcal{G}$ may need re-pinning. Pre-registered as a known limitation.
- **Multi-agent or team hierarchies.** The brief asks about *agent* hierarchy. If the intended sense is a team hierarchy (e.g., specialized sub-agents with delegation), the design would need to be re-specified; this remains a flagged design-stage interpretation.
- **Raider AI sophistication.** Raiders are environment-controlled and rule-based in the Specimen. If a real engine uses learned raider AI, additional threats apply (construct: raider is itself a learner that may exploit architectures differently) — flagged, not addressed in this design.
- **Compute actuals vs targets.** Compute estimates in §11 are design targets. Actual wall-clock depends on the bound engine's per-step cost.
- **No experiments have been run.** This document is a design specification only.

(See \u00a74 for capacity matching.)\n\n---\n\n## 2. Specimen Sandbox \u2014 Mechanic Contract\n\nThe Specimen is a formal mechanical specification, not a runnable artifact. The design can be bound to any real game iff that game's mechanics satisfy this contract.\n\n### 2.1 World\n\n- Discrete 2D toroidal grid, $32\\times 32$, eight pre-defined layouts in $\\mathcal{M}$ (one resource-clusters-near-base, one resource-clusters-distant, etc.).\n- Agents: one player unit; base with HP/HP_base; up to $N_{\\max}=24$ raider units.\n- Resource nodes: harvested for score increments and HP restoration.\n\n### 2.2 State & dynamics\n\n- State $s_t = (\\text{world}_t,\\text{player}_t,\\text{base}_t,\\text{raiders}_t, S_t)$.\n- Update rule is deterministic given $(\\text{state}, \\text{action}, \\text{RNG draw})$.\n- Per-step cost invariant across architectures (verified by side-channel timestamp on a held-out calibration harness).\n\n### 2.3 Actions & observations\n\n- Primitive action set $\\mathcal{A}_\\text{prim} = \\{\\text{move-N,E,S,W},\\text{harvest},\\text{fortify},\\text{attack},\\text{idle}\\}$ (8 actions).\n- Observation vector: spatial window around player, base HP, $S_t$, raider counts by distance bin, time-since-last-event.\n- Identical for both architectures.\n\n### 2.4 Score $S_t$\n\n```\nS_t = S_{t-1}\n    + c_h * (resources_harvested_at_t)\n    + c_m * (monument_value_if_completed)\n    + c_s * (1 if alive and base intact, else 0)\n```\n\nConstants $(c_h, c_m, c_s)$ pinned; reported in the Specimen contract register.\n\n### 2.5 Pirate-invasion mechanic\n\n- Default state: $\\text{RAID}_t = \\text{false}$.\n- Regime-specific dispatch rules (\u00a73) determine when $\\text{RAID}_t := \\text{true}$.\n- While $\\text{RAID}_t = \\text{true}$: spawn waves of size $W$ at distance band $d$, each raider dealing DPS $dpa$ for duration $D$ waves. $W, d, dpa, D$ pinned in regime definitions.\n- Raiders expire after $D$ waves or after inflicting cumulative damage cap.\n\n### 2.6 Terminal failure\n\n- $\\tau = t$ if at step $t$: player HP $\\le 0$ **or** base HP $\\le 0$.\n- Else $\\tau = H$, $\\delta = 0$ (right-censored).\n\n### 2.7 Initial-condition pins\n\n- $S_0$ pinned below $T_{\\text{lo}}$, identical across all cells.\n- Identical initial resources, identical initial base HP, identical player HP.\n- Identical map layouts drawn once from $\\mathcal{M}$, then held fixed across architectures.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Trigger Regimes\n\n| Regime | Dispatch rule | Cadence | Intensity |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{off}}$ | $\\text{RAID}_t \\equiv \\text{false}$ for all $t$ | none | none |\n| $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{single}}$ | If $\\neg\\text{RAID}_{t-1}$ and $S_t \\ge T$, set $\\text{RAID}_t = \\text{true}$ for one wave of size $W_0$ | one-shot | constant $W_0$ |\n| $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{period}}$ | If $S_t \\ge T$ and $(t - t_{\\text{first\\_cross}}) \\mod K = 0$, spawn one wave | periodic, period $K$ | constant $W_0$ per wave |\n| $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{scaled}}$ | On first crossing spawn wave of size $W_0$; if wave resolved and $S_t \\ge T$ still, re-arm to $\\lceil \\alpha (S_t - T) \\rceil$ if larger | one-shot + escalator | $W \\propto \\lceil \\alpha (S_t - T)\\rceil$ |\n\n**Defaults (pre-registered):** $K = 200$, $\\alpha = 0.1$, $W_0 = 6$, raid DPS-profile and distance pin in contract register. **Robustness:** $K \\in \\{100, 200, 400\\}$ and $\\alpha \\in \\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\\}$ reported as secondary sweeps in \u00a79.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Agent Architectures & Capacity Matching (Hard Control)\n\n### 4.1 Hierarchical architecture $\\mathcal{A}_{\\text{hier}}$\n\n- **High-level policy** $\\pi_{\\text{high}}(g \\mid o_{t:k_{\\text{hl}}})$, discrete-softmax over $\\mathcal{G}$.\n- **Low-level policy** $\\pi_{\\text{low}}(a_t \\mid o_t, g)$, with primitive action space $\\mathcal{A}_\\text{prim}$.\n- High-level emits $g$ at steps $t \\in \\{0, k_{\\text{hl}}, 2k_{\\text{hl}}, \\dots\\}$; low-level emits one $a_t$ every step, including between high-level decisions (the previously committed $g$ persists).\n- A separate value head $V_{\\text{combined}}$ is used for training only and does not change the action distribution shape.\n\n### 4.2 Non-hierarchical (flat) architecture $\\mathcal{A}_{\\text{flat}}$\n\n- **Single policy** $\\pi_{\\text{flat}}(a_t \\mid o_t)$ over $\\mathcal{A}_\\text{prim}$.\n- A value head is included to mirror training conditions.\n\n### 4.3 Capacity-matching control (hard)\n\nTo avoid confounding architecture with capacity, the following are **mandatory and pre-registered**:\n\n| Axis | Constraint |\n|---|---|\n| Total trainable parameters $P$ | $\\lvert P_{\\text{hier}} - P_{\\text{flat}}\\rvert / P_{\\text{flat}} \\le 5\\%$ |\n| Optimizer family | identical (Adam) |\n| Optimizer hyperparameters | identical $(\\eta, \\beta_1, \\beta_2, \\epsilon)$ |\n| Update count (env steps per gradient step, total gradient steps) | identical |\n| Replay memory | shared buffer length, identical sampling distribution |\n| Exploration schedule | identical $(\\epsilon_{\\text{start}}, \\epsilon_{\\text{end}}, \\text{decay})$ |\n| Batch size | identical |\n| Discount $\\gamma$, TD$(\\lambda)$ | identical |\n| Random seed for init | shared seed and deterministic init order |\n\n**Tolerance justification ($\\pm 5\\%$).** Implementations of \"matched capacity\" must contend with discretization of layer widths, embedding tables for $\\mathcal{G}$, and head/tail asymmetries. A $\\pm 5\\%$ window on $P$ is tight enough to prevent gross capacity confounds (literature precedent in paired-network ablation design typically uses 5\u201310%) while permitting the natural parameter-count deltas introduced by embedding $\\lvert\\mathcal{G}\\rvert = 4$ discrete subgoals into the hierarchical encoder. As a robustness check, \u00a79 reports results within a $\\pm 2\\%$ tight tolerance on a held-out subset; deviations in primary outcome between the $5\\%$ and $2\\%$ tolerances would be flagged and reported narratively.\n\n### 4.4 Action-budget and timing-parity control\n\n- Both architectures emit exactly one primitive action per environment step.\n- Hierarchical emits $g$ at the pre-pinned $k_{\\text{hl}}$ cadence; no additional actions, no skipping, no extra reads.\n- Decision latency is irrelevant because both act synchronously with the environment step.\n\n---\n\n## 5. A priori Causal Rationale per Regime\n\nFor each regime, the design names the expected direction of the architecture effect, the mechanism, and the substantive alternative (the design must be able to detect either).\n\n### 5.1 $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{off}}$ \u2014 no trigger\n\n- **Expected direction (this design's prior):** $\\tau_{\\text{hier}} \\approx \\tau_{\\text{flat}}$; either small flat underperformance from subgoal-switching overhead, or small hierarchical overperformance if subgoaling decomposes healthy-behaviour subproblems.\n- **Mechanism:** no external stress tests the architecture's ability to schedule. Both controllers should maintain a baseline \"gather without dying\" loop.\n- **Substantive alternative:** Hierarchical suffers from macro-level commitment to a subgoal across $k_{\\text{hl}}$ steps when the optimal action is to immediately replan, so $\\tau_{\\text{hier}} < \\tau_{\\text{flat}}$.\n- **Purpose in design:** arm acts as a control on capacity-only effects absent triggers; any Architecture main effect that survives only in regimes with triggers is interpretable as a triggered-mechanic interaction.\n\n### 5.2 $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{single}}$ \u2014 one wave at threshold\n\n- **Expected direction (prior):** $\\tau_{\\text{hier}} > \\tau_{\\text{flat}}$ by a moderate margin.\n- **Mechanism:** the high-level controller can pre-commit to `fortify` (or stay in `fortify`) just before the crossed-threshold event if it has been collecting resources toward $T$; the flat policy must learn this anticipation purely from feature engineering over $(o_t, S_t)$.\n- **Substantive alternative:** flat policy learns a sharp, low-latency mapping from $(S_{t-T}, \\text{trajectory})$ to fortify action, and the hierarchical controller's fixed $k_{\\text{hl}}$ cadence prevents it from anticipating the final pre-trigger decision in time.\n\n### 5.3 $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{period}}$ \u2014 repeated raids\n\n- **Expected direction (prior):** $\\tau_{\\text{hier}} > \\tau_{\\text{flat}}$ by a wider margin than $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{single}}$; staggered adaptation benefits subgoal cycling.\n- **Mechanism:** multi-step planning horizon at the macro level lets the controller weave `fortify` and `gather` in alternation across periods, exploiting high-level cadence; flat controller may thrash between conflicting primitive reflexes.\n- **Substantive alternative:** commitment cost dominates \u2014 $\\pi_{\\text{high}}$ cannot reverse a stale subgoal within the $k_{\\text{hl}}$ window, so the agent under-responds during the next wave's early phase; flat wins.\n\n### 5.4 $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{scaled}}$ \u2014 escalating intensity\n\n- **Expected direction (prior):** $\\tau_{\\text{hier}} > \\tau_{\\text{flat}}$.\n- **Mechanism:** hierarchical policy's subgoal space includes `evade` and `counterattack` as well as `gather` and `fortify`, so intensifying pressure maps cleanly onto a high-level switch; flat policy must learn a *continuous* scalar mapping from stress features to action probabilities, which is a harder credit-assignment problem.\n- **Substantive alternative:** both architectures fail comparably under sustained DPS ramps; once any raid wave penetrates, the marginal value of architecture is small.\n\n### 5.5 Causal graph\n\n```\nArchitecture (HIER/FLAT)  \u2500\u2510\n                            \u251c\u2500\u25ba Behaviour pattern \u2500\u25ba Triggered event interaction \u2500\u25ba Survival \u03c4\nTriggering regime (4 arms) \u2500\u2518\n      \u2191\nDeterministic schedule from paired seed \u03be  (controls world init, event timing, all draws)\n```\n\nThe Architecture \u00d7 Regime interaction is the primary contrast of interest; the schedule contamination is closed by paired-seed replay (see \u00a76).\n\n---\n\n## 6. Experimental Design\n\n### 6.1 Factorial structure\n\n- **Between-subjects factor:** Architecture ($\\mathcal{A}_{\\text{hier}}$ vs $\\mathcal{A}_{\\text{flat}}$).\n- **Within-subjects factor:** Regime ($\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{off}}, \\mathcal{R}_{\\text{single}}, \\mathcal{R}_{\\text{period}}, \\mathcal{R}_{\\text{scaled}}$).\n- **Threshold factor (robustness):** $T \\in \\{T_{\\text{lo}}, T_{\\text{mid}}, T_{\\text{hi}}\\}$, with $T_{\\text{mid}}$ used for the *primary* analysis. The other two thresholds are reported as a robustness sweep.\n- Cells per threshold: $2 \\times 4 = 8$. Total architecture cells: $2 \\times 4 \\times 3 = 24$, but the primary analysis pool is $8$ cells \u00d7 $T_{\\text{mid}}$ alone.\n\n### 6.2 Seed pairing\n\n- Each seed index $i \\in \\{1, \\dots, n_s\\}$ defines one seed string $\\xi_i$.\n- For both architectures, the same $\\xi_i$ determines: (i) world init, (ii) resource distribution, (iii) initial player & base state, (iv) any stochastic event timing that is *not* regime-defined (so the only regime-varying RNG draws come from the regime itself).\n- Within $\\xi_i$, the four regimes are presented in a **chequerboard (counterbalanced) order** across seeds, so any residual order effects are decorrelated from architecture.\n\n### 6.3 Pre-registered defaults (from researcher authorization)\n\n| Parameter | Default | Justification |\n|---|---|---|\n| $n_s$ (seeds per architecture cell) | $64$ | Achieves $\\ge 30$ uncensored deaths in the smallest cell at $T_{\\text{mid}}$ under realistic survival curves; power computed in \u00a710. |\n| $H$ (horizon) | $5000$ steps | Long enough that $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{period}}$ and $\\mathcal{R}_{\\text{scaled}}$ realize multi-event trajectories in most cells; short enough that compute remains tractable. |\n| $T_{\\text{mid}}, T_{\\text{lo}}, T_{\\text{hi}}$ | e.g. $\\{0.45 S_{\\max}, 0.30 S_{\\max}, 0.60 S_{\\max}\\}$ calibrated so that half of seeds cross at $T_{\\text{mid}}$ by step $H$ under $\\mathcal{A}_{\\text{flat}}, \\mathcal{R}_{\\text{off}}$. |\n| Map pool $\\mathcal{M}$ | $8$ fixed layouts, drawn once before the run | Avoids map-induced confound of architecture-with-layout. |\n\n### 6.4 What is controlled across all cells\n\n- Identical $\\mathcal{A}_\\text{prim}$; identical observation space; identical per-step budget; identical Specimen parameter pins.\n- Identical optimizer, exploration, batch size, replay memory, training updates.\n- Identical $S_0$, identical map layouts.\n- Identical RNG seed string assigned to architecture & regime at the trial level via the seed protocol.\n\n### 6.5 What *varies*\n\n- Across rows of the $2 \\times 4$ factorial, only (architecture, regime) vary.\n- Across threshold-sweep cells, only $T$ varies; everything else held.\n\n### 6.6 What *cannot* be controlled (and is acknowledged)\n\n- Library-level RNG draws from non-rule-driven system paths (network is disabled; this is moot here). Documented in \u00a712.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Outcome Metric \u2014 Survival Duration\n\n**Primary outcome variable:** $\\tau \\in [0, H]$, the step at which terminal failure first occurs.\n\n**Definition in the Specimen:**\n\n$$\\tau = \\begin{cases} \\min\\{t : \\text{playerHP}_t \\le 0 \\;\\lor\\; \\text{baseHP}_t \\le 0\\}, & \\text{otherwise} \\\\ H, & \\text{if no failure by step } H \\end{cases}$$\n\n**Censoring indicator:** $\\delta = \\mathbb{1}[\\tau < H]$.\n\n**Right-censoring rule:** when $\\tau = H$, the censored observation contributes under standard survival-analysis weighting; KM and Cox estimators handle this natively.\n\n**Censoring at horizon cap.** A right-censoring fraction under $25\\%$ is targeted per cell to avoid informative-censoring bias; if a cell exceeds $30\\%$ censoring, KM tail extrapolation (exponential tail fit on the last decile) is reported as a robustness view in \u00a79. The horizon bound $H = 5000$ is set with this target in mind.\n\n**Auxiliary outcomes (secondary, pre-registered):**\n\n- $\\tau_{\\text{to-event}}$: steps from episode start to first event (single, periodic wave 1, scaled wave 1). Diagnostic only \u2014 not a Primary.\n- $n_{\\text{waves-survived}}$: count of waves survived before terminal failure.\n- $\\text{score-ceiling}_\\tau = S_\\tau$: terminal score.\n\nThese are reported to characterize mechanism, not to adjudicate the primary question.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Pre-registered Analysis Decision Tree\n\n```\nPRIMARY OUTCOME\n  \u2514\u2500 \u03c4 (survival duration in [0, H]), right-censored at H\n\nPRIMARY CONTRAST\n  \u2514\u2500 Architecture \u00d7 Regime interaction (does \u03c4_hier \u2212 \u03c4_flat depend on regime?)\n\nPRIMARY TEST\n  \u2514\u2500 Mixed-effects Cox proportional-hazards model:\n       h(t | X, \u03be_i) = h_0(t) \u00b7 exp(\u03b2_arch \u00b7 arch + \u03b2_regime \u00b7 regime\n                                    + \u03b2_int \u00b7 (arch \u00d7 regime) + u_\u03be_i)\n     random intercept u_\u03be_i ~ N(0, \u03c3\u00b2_\u03be) on seed \u03be_i\n     Reports: HR_arch, HR_regime, HR_int each with 95% CI; p_int pre-registered\n  \u2514\u2500 If Schoenfeld residuals reject proportional-hazards assumption:\n     \u2192 Stratified Cox by regime (collapse interaction test).\n     Pre-registered fallback.\n  \u2514\u2500 Non-parametric check: stratified log-rank test across regimes, by architecture.\n\nSECONDARY CONTRASTS (pre-registered list, Holm-Bonferroni adjusted)\n  1. Architecture main effect (collapsed across regime)\n  2. Regime main effect (collapsed across architecture)\n  3. Within-architecture pairwise regime contrasts (3 per architecture, 6 total)\n  4. Subgroup HR at each regime level\n\nEXPLORATORY CONTRASTS (not pre-registered, marked exploratory in any write-up)\n  - Threshold-level subgroup analyses\n  - Seed-cluster analyses (leave-one-seed-out)\n  - Wave-count covariate models\n\nMISSING DATA HANDLING\n  \u2514\u2500 Design is seed-complete: missingness equals zero by construction.\n  \u2514\u2500 In the event of run-level failures (e.g. Specimen contract violation\n     detected post-hoc), the affected seed is excluded and a sensitivity\n     re-run is reported with results from a deviance threshold in \u00a79.\n\nCENSORING TREATMENT\n  \u2514\u2500 Right-censoring at H handled by Cox and KM estimators natively.\n  \u2514\u2500 Censoring-fraction diagnostic per cell; >30% triggers exponential-tail\n     robustness view (KM tail extrapolation).\n\nMULTIPLICITY RULE\n  \u2514\u2500 Holm-Bonferroni step-down over the 4 secondary contrast families.\n  \u2514\u2500 Primary interaction tested at \u03b1 = 0.05 and reported regardless of\n     multiplicity adjustment.\n\nEFFECT-SIZE REPORTING\n  \u2514\u2500 Hazard ratio with 95% CI is the primary effect size for \u03c4.\n  \u2514\u2500 Cohen's d on log(\u03c4 + 1) reported as a familiar secondary effect size.\n  \u2514\u2500 Median survival and 25th/75th percentiles reported per cell.\n\nROBUSTNESS PRIORITIZATION\n  \u2514\u2500 Pre-registered order: (a) threshold sweep, (b) capacity-tolerance tightening,\n     (c) censoring-fraction sensitivity, (d) leave-one-seed-out, (e) bootstrap CI\n     over seeds.\n```\n\n**Decision rule for adjudicating the primary question.** The question is about whether the *triggering of mechanics* affects the survival of hierarchical vs non-hierarchical agents. We adjudicate as follows:\n\n- If the Architecture \u00d7 Regime interaction in the Cox model reaches $\\alpha = 0.05$ with $|HR_{\\text{int}}| \\not\\approx 1$, the answer is **yes** (the survival difference between architectures depends on regime).\n- If the interaction fails but Architecture main effect survives Holm-corrected secondary tests *and* all four regimes show monotone direction-consistent HIER-vs-FLAT HRs, report **provisionally yes** with the architecture main effect conditional on regime.\n- If neither interaction nor main effect reaches significance, report **insufficient evidence** and explicitly identify power under $n_s = 64$ (computed in \u00a710).\n\n---\n\n## 9. Robustness & Sensitivity\n\n| Check | What it varies | Decision criteria |\n|---|---|---|\n| Threshold sweep | $T \\in \\{T_{\\text{lo}}, T_{\\text{mid}}, T_{\\text{hi}}\\}$ | Primary direction of $HR_{\\text{int}}$ is consistent across at least 2 of 3 thresholds |\n| Capacity-tolerance tightening | $\\pm 5\\% \\to \\pm 2\\%$ on parameter count | Direction preserved; magnitude variation reported as confidence band |\n| Subgoal cadence sweep | $k_{\\text{hl}} \\in \\{25, 50, 100\\}$ (hierarchical only) | Direction preserved; magnitude reported as robustness band |\n| Cadence $K$ sweep | $K \\in \\{100, 200, 400\\}$ (periodic regime) | Direction preserved |\n| Intensity $\\alpha$ sweep | $\\alpha \\in \\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\\}$ (scaled regime) | Direction preserved |\n| Censoring sensitivity | KM tail extrapolation if censoring $> 30\\%$ | Disagreement triggers caveat narrative |\n| Leave-one-seed-out | Repeat with one seed removed | No single seed drives the effect |\n| Bootstrap CIs | Resample seeds 10,000 times | 95% CI on HR; reported with point estimate |\n| Map robustness | Repeat with maps sampled from a held-out pool of 4 | Direction preserved across maps |\n\nSpecific defaults: $H=5000$, $n_s=64$ \u2014 these are sensitivity-tunable. \u00a710 considers $n_s \\in \\{32, 64, 96\\}$ and $H \\in \\{3000, 5000, 8000\\}$.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Sample-Size Justification\n\n### 10.1 Pre-registered prospective rule\n\nEach architecture cell must reach **at least 30 uncensored deaths (i.e., $\\delta = 1$)** *or* the Kaplan\u2013Meier standard error on the median survival must fall below a pre-specified precision target under realistic survival curves.\n\n### 10.2 Worked power estimate (analytical, not empirical)\n\nAssume an exponential baseline survival with median $\\tau_0 = 1500$ steps, $H = 5000$, so expected uncensoring fraction $\\approx 1 - \\exp(-H/\\tau_0) \\approx 1 - \\exp(-3.33) \\approx 0.964$. With $n_s = 64$ per cell, expected deaths $\\approx 62$, well above the 30 threshold. If the relevant survival is shorter (e.g., $\\tau_0 = 700$, which models the worst regime), uncensoring $\\approx 1 - \\exp(-5000/700) \\approx 0.999$, so $n_s = 64$ again exceeds the 30-death threshold.\n\nFor Cox detection of an interaction effect size of $HR_{\\text{int}} = 1.5$ with two-sided $\\alpha = 0.05$, power $\\approx 0.85$ at $n_s = 64$ per architecture cell under the rule-of-thumb that $10$ events-per-coefficient are needed (Hsieh\u2013Lavori-style). Realized event counts substantially exceed that under any of the survival curves above. Smaller interactions ($HR_{\\text{int}} = 1.25$) would require $n_s \\approx 96$ to retain $0.80$ power.\n\n### 10.3 Sensitivity to defaults\n\n| $(n_s, H)$ combination | Satisfies \u226530 deaths / cell? | Power vs $HR_{\\text{int}}=1.5$ | Power vs $HR_{\\text{int}}=1.25$ |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| $(32, 3000)$ | Boundary; report flag | $\\approx 0.60$ | $\\approx 0.25$ |\n| **(64, 5000)** (default) | Yes | $\\approx 0.85$ | $\\approx 0.45$ |\n| $(96, 5000)$ | Yes | $\\approx 0.95$ | $\\approx 0.65$ |\n| $(64, 8000)$ | Yes | $\\approx 0.88$ | $\\approx 0.50$ |\n\nThe pre-registered default $(64, 5000)$ is selected as the design's primary anchor; \u00a79 reports sensitivity to both $n_s$ and $H$.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Feasibility\n\nThis section reports numerical *targets*, not execution claims. All values are design-stage estimates derived from the Specimen contract; binding to a real engine changes them.\n\n### 11.1 Compute-hours target\n\n- **Per-trial simulation time** (Specimen reference speed, Java/Python reference profile):\n  - $H = 5000$ steps \u00d7 $\\approx 50\\,\\mu$s/step (StepsC++ reference) $\\Rightarrow$ $\\approx 0.25$ s/trial.\n- **Per architecture cell:** $n_s \\cdot 4 \\text{ regimes} \\cdot 0.25 \\text{ s} = 64 \\cdot 4 \\cdot 0.25 = 64$ s.\n- **All primary cells:** $2$ arch \u00d7 $4$ reg \u00d7 $64$ s = $512$ s \u2248 $0.14$ hours of pure simulation.\n- **All cells including threshold sweep:** $0.14 \\times 3 = 0.43$ hours.\n- **Policy training (offline, not part of per-trial compute):**\n  - Estimate: $4$ hours per trained policy on 24-thread CPU (no GPU required).\n  - Policies required: $2$ architectures \u00d7 $1$ training corpus = $2$ policies.\n  - Total training: $\\approx 8$ hours.\n  - Note: if the Specimen is bound to a learned-agent framework that requires retraining per regime, multiply accordingly; in the default Specimen, regime is an environment configuration toggle, not an agent retraining condition.\n- **Total runtime target:** $\\approx 8$\u2013$10$ hours wall-clock to produce primary analysis on a 24-core CPU.\n\n### 11.2 Wall-clock rationale\n\n- 24-core CPU affinity is sufficient because: (i) trials are independent across seeds and can be parallelized one trial per core; (ii) per-trial memory is small (\u00a711.3).\n- Wall-clock target is dominated by training (8h) over per-trial simulation (~0.5h).
